strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: enabling a compact VLM driving agent to request additional visual evidence when its initial observations are insufficient.
The hybrid text/tool formulation, four-tool perception suite, and three-stage SFT/FCM-RL/AMS-RL pipeline form a coherent system and are explained with clear figures.

DriveAgent-R1 obtains substantial gains on SUP-AD, including 70.11% first-frame joint accuracy and 44.06% sequence-average joint accuracy, and the paper includes useful stage-wise, forced-mode, and image-removal ablations.
Using a 3B backbone is practically appealing, and the manuscript is generally well organized and readable.
weaknesses: The main state-of-the-art comparison is not controlled: DriveAgent-R1 is trained extensively on the target task, whereas all competing VLMs are evaluated through one-shot prompting. Task-trained prior methods, a comparably fine-tuned backbone, and compute-matched standard-GRPO baselines are absent, so the claimed superiority over larger models is not persuasive.

Tool use provides privileged additional inputs—high-resolution views, five seconds of history, depth estimation, and outputs from an external 3D detector. There are no input- or compute-matched baselines that simply process these observations, nor per-tool, full-resolution, history-only, or fixed-tool-policy ablations. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed specifically to active selection or MP-GRPO.

The central efficiency benefit of hybrid thinking is not demonstrated. The paper reports no latency, FLOPs, tool-call frequency, throughput, or accuracy-cost tradeoff. Forced tool use actually exceeds free selection in first-frame accuracy (71.23% versus 70.11%), making the value of adaptive selection unclear.

Mode Selection Accuracy is weakly validated: its target is constructed retrospectively from the same model's forced-mode outcomes, ties default to text mode, and neither mode prevalence nor trivial always-text/always-tool baselines are reported. Thus, 65.93% MSA may not indicate meaningful selection ability.

Evaluation is limited to one random 1,500-sample split of one dataset, with no scene- or route-disjoint leakage analysis, additional datasets, closed-loop simulation, collision metrics, robustness tests, or real-time evaluation. Open-loop classification of four meta-actions from a keyframe does not substantiate the manuscript's strong reliability and safety claims.

Several metrics are insufficiently specified or validated. The construction of relaxed joint accuracy is ambiguous, while H-Score depends on a proprietary Gemini judge without the evaluation prompt, decoding protocol, repeated judgments, human agreement, or sensitivity analysis. No confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed learning contributions: the full three-stage model receives more optimization than reduced variants, and there is no equal-compute standard-GRPO or alternative curriculum baseline. Likewise, a larger degradation after removing images establishes modality dependence, not groundedness, robustness, or causal use of the requested evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits the size of the RL set, data-partition thresholds, RL iteration counts and learning rates, reward weights and numerical schedules, GRPO/KL and sampling settings, prompts, inference decoding parameters, random seeds, and any code or checkpoint release.

The novelty is primarily a task-specific combination of existing tool-augmented multimodal reasoning, hybrid reasoning, and GRPO. MP-GRPO appears to change group composition rather than introduce a clearly analyzed objective, and label-conditioned teacher rationales are not tested for faithfulness or interpretability.

There is no statistical robustness analysis despite stochastic decoding at temperature 0.7. No confidence intervals, repeated training/evaluation seeds, or significance tests are reported. weaknesses: The evaluation does not validate autonomous-driving safety or planning quality. It is an offline classification task that imitates one realized future trajectory using a coarse action vocabulary; many other actions may be valid. There is no closed-loop driving, collision rate, route completion, comfort, rule-compliance, or trajectory evaluation. Consequently, the claims of safer and more reliable driving are substantially stronger than the evidence.

The approximately 50% human accuracy reinforces concerns that the target is ambiguous or noisy. Only three drivers are used, each evaluates a different third of the data, and no repeated annotation, inter-rater agreement, or adjudication is reported. Moreover, humans receive only the front image whereas the agent can access surrounding/history views and learned perception tools, making the human-level comparison poorly controlled.

The headline comparison against GPT-5 is not apples-to-apples. DriveAgent-R1 receives extensive domain training on 530K VQA pairs plus SFT and RL, whereas general baselines are evaluated one-shot and closed models are explicitly placed in a no-thinking mode. The claimed 3B footprint also excludes the depth and 3D-detection models and their computational cost.

The internal split is insufficiently specified: the test set is described as a random sample from the same 35K-clip collection used for training, without confirming clip-, scene-, route-, or location-disjointness. Nearby frames could therefore leak across splits. The proprietary data, generated annotations, code, checkpoints, and most exact training hyperparameters are unavailable, seriously limiting reproducibility.

The evidence for genuine visual grounding is weak. A larger accuracy drop after removing images is an out-of-distribution dependence test, not proof that tool evidence causally improves correct decisions. Missing controls include shuffled or contradictory tool outputs, irrelevant-tool interventions, matched-information/token-budget baselines, tool-correctness measurements, and complete per-tool ablations. One showcased example even queries the 3D detector for a “bus” while attributing discovery of pedestrians to that call.

Reported improvements lack confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or training-seed variation. Several central gains are only about 1–3 points and evaluation uses stochastic sampling at temperature 0.7, so their robustness is unknown. The latency analysis likewise omits dispersion and does not clearly state whether all detector/depth execution and transfer costs are included.

Mode Selection Accuracy is circular and model-dependent: the “optimal” mode is whichever forced mode happens to score higher for that sample. The paper does not specify repeated sampling, tie handling, or expected-mode performance, so MSA is not an independent measure of scene complexity or correct routing.

The reward definition has a technical problem that needs justification. With substitution cost 1−I(match)w and normalized weights that can exceed 1, correct matches can have negative edit cost and similarity above 1, while exact matches with weights below 1 incur positive cost. In AMS-RL, the tool reward also vanishes whenever a four-sample group contains no text trajectory, creating a poorly characterized and potentially mode-collapsing signal.

Novelty is not established convincingly relative to prior tool-augmented driving work such as AgentThink and existing hybrid-reasoning approaches. MP-GRPO appears primarily to place forced samples from two modes into one GRPO normalization group; stronger direct baselines and a sharper account of the technical distinction are needed.

The paper omits important autonomous-driving ethics and safety considerations, including dataset provenance, privacy/anonymization of real-world imagery, consent or licensing, deployment misuse, and safeguards against acting on erroneous tool outputs. The single qualitative failure analysis does not address these broader risks.

weaknesses: The evaluation does not substantiate the central autonomous-driving, safety, reliability, or deployment claims. It is an offline imitation task predicting four coarse actions from recorded observations, with no closed-loop simulation, collision metrics, intervention analysis, robustness testing, or real-vehicle evaluation. Moreover, the reported 6.74-second adaptive inference latency exceeds the two-second action interval, directly weakening the claim of deployment readiness.

Ground truth is generated automatically from future ego trajectories and then refined by GPT-4.1, with no independent manual quality audit. The refinement prompt is required to preserve every speed label, so it cannot correct ambiguous speed annotations. A single observed trajectory is also not a unique optimal plan. The low human agreement with these labels—approximately 48–49%—is evidence of ambiguity or label noise rather than a meaningful human driving ceiling.

The claimed human-level comparison is not credible. Each of only three drivers labels a different third of the data, preventing inter-rater agreement measurement, and humans receive only the front image, speed, and navigation command while the tool-enabled model can access additional views, history, zoomed imagery, depth, and detection outputs. Agreement with synthetic labels should not be called human driving proficiency.

The evaluation metric is insufficiently validated. Its asymmetric relaxed matching awards partial credit to predictions deemed 'safer,' potentially favoring systematic over-braking, yet results are called joint accuracy. No class distribution, majority-policy baseline, per-action recall, safety-critical error breakdown, calibration analysis, or exact full-sequence accuracy is reported.

Experimental controls and statistical evidence are weak. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple training seeds, even though several claimed improvements are around 0.4–1.3 points. The paper does not establish scene- or clip-disjoint Drive-Internal splits, prevent temporally adjacent leakage, identify the selected 2K nuScenes examples, or explain why only a subset is evaluated.

Comparisons to GPT-5 and other general VLMs are not well controlled: DriveAgent-R1 receives extensive task-specific supervised and RL training, whereas those systems are evaluated one-shot. More relevant specialized driving planners and tool-using driving agents cited by the paper are not compared. This also makes the parameter-count comparison misleading.

The novelty is limited and insufficiently positioned. Selective visual tools, tool-augmented multimodal reasoning, hybrid reasoning, and staged GRPO are established ideas; the cited AgentThink work is already explicitly described as tool-augmented chain-of-thought for autonomous driving. MP-GRPO appears mainly to force an equal number of samples per mode before ordinary group normalization, without theoretical or sufficiently strong empirical evidence of a distinct algorithmic contribution.

Several technical definitions are incomplete or inconsistent. The main text describes a margin-based tool reward, whereas the appendix uses a per-call cost; free mode selection can produce groups with no text trajectory and therefore no contrastive reward; MSA depends on a noisy post-hoc 'optimal mode' whose sampling and tie handling are unspecified; and the weighted Levenshtein definition gives nonzero costs to correct common actions and negative costs to correct rare actions. The GRPO objective, format reward, optimization settings, thresholds, and multiple data-filtering mechanisms are not reproducibly specified.

The evidence for active perception is not sufficiently isolated. The active system may access historical and higher-resolution imagery unavailable to passive baselines, so the asserted identical information ceiling is questionable. There are no quantitative per-tool ablations, tool-selection frequencies, tool-error measurements, or complete tool-runtime accounting. Figure 11 even queries the detector for 'bus' but claims that the resulting call detects pedestrians, undermining the qualitative evidence.

Removing images and observing a larger performance drop demonstrates dependence on images, not that the visual evidence is correctly used or that reasoning is faithful. Generated chain-of-thought is not independently validated for faithfulness, and most qualitative cases are cherry-picked successes.

Reproducibility is poor because the principal dataset is private, and no code, model checkpoints, generated labels, split lists, or release commitment is provided. The proprietary VQA benchmark is generated and evaluated using automated models without independent human validation.

For a safety-critical application, the manuscript lacks an adequate broader-impact or ethics discussion covering foreseeable deployment misuse, dataset privacy and consent, demographic or geographic bias, tool failures, and the danger of interpreting this offline benchmark as evidence of real-world driving safety. The unresolved visual-conflict failure mode is particularly consequential.

Consequently, claims of improved safety, reliability, human driving proficiency, and deployment readiness are unsupported.

The benchmark has questionable validity for planning. A single logged behavior is treated as ground truth despite many potentially safe alternatives, and the asymmetric relaxed-speed score rewards conservative deviations without demonstrating safety. The human study uses only one driver per sample, reports no inter-rater agreement or uncertainty, and gives humans only the front view while the evaluated agent can access extra views, history, and perception tools.

Novelty and comparative evidence are insufficient. Tool-augmented multimodal reasoning and adaptive hybrid reasoning are established ideas, and the paper does not convincingly distinguish itself from directly relevant cited work such as AgentThink. It omits specialist driving and tool-use baselines such as AgentThink, Drive-R1, and AlphaDrive, instead emphasizing comparisons between a task-trained system and generic models queried one-shot, with closed models additionally placed in a no-thinking mode.

Dataset integrity and reproducibility are major concerns. The Drive-Internal test set is described only as a random sample from the same collection used for training, without confirming clip-, route-, or scene-level separation; near-duplicate leakage is therefore unresolved. The provenance and overlap controls for the one-million-frame alignment corpus are also absent. The internal datasets are unavailable, and key training hyperparameters, filtering thresholds, judge-model details, tool configurations, model snapshots, and sampling seeds are missing.

Most reported advantages are small and lack confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or multi-seed results, despite stochastic evaluation at temperature 0.7. For example, active retrieval improves over Passive-SV by only 1.29 points, while several claimed GPT-5 and human comparisons differ by roughly 1–3 points. The paper therefore does not establish that these rankings are robust.

The evidence for genuine visual grounding is weak. A larger degradation after removing images does not show that selected tools provide causally relevant evidence or that generated rationales are faithful. There are no corrupted/shuffled-tool controls, tool-call success metrics, mode and call-frequency statistics, or detailed per-tool and long-tail-category analyses. The qualitative evidence even contains an internal inconsistency: Figure 11 queries the detector for a bus but attributes discovery of pedestrians to that call.

Several technical definitions are under-specified or inconsistent. MSA defines an optimal mode through stochastic forced-mode outcomes but gives no tie rule or estimation protocol. The main text describes a margin-based tool reward, whereas the appendix specifies a per-call-cost formula; groups without text trajectories receive no tool reward. MP-GRPO is not compared directly with standard GRPO under matched sampling, and combining forced samples from different conditional modes under one group normalization is not adequately justified.

The 3B and efficiency claims exclude the parameters, memory, and execution cost of the external depth and 3D-detection systems. The passive baseline receives fixed current views, whereas active retrieval can access historical frames and higher-resolution evidence, so the claimed identical information ceiling and latency comparison are not fully controlled. The paper also lacks adequate discussion of privacy, dataset licensing and geographic bias, or the risks of presenting an unvalidated high-stakes driving system as deployment-ready.
